facts.statement: The genus Quinkana was described by Molnar in 1981.
facts.quote: authority: Molnar, 1981

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Quinkana is Quinkana fortirostrum.
facts.quote: type_species: Quinkana fortirostrum

facts.statement: Four species are currently recognized within the genus Quinkana: Q. fortirostrum, Q. timara, Q. babarra, and Q. meboldi.
facts.quote: subdivision: * Quinkana fortirostrum Molnar, 1981 (type) Quinkana timara Megirian, 1994 Quinkana babarra Willis & Mackness, 1996 Quinkana meboldi Willis, 1997

facts.statement: Quinkana lived in Australia from approximately 25 million years ago until about 20,000 years ago.
facts.quote: lived in Australia from about 25 million to about 20,000 years ago

facts.statement: The majority of Quinkana fossils have been discovered in Queensland, Australia.
facts.quote: with the majority of fossils having been found in Queensland

facts.statement: Quinkana is distinguished by a combination of ziphodont teeth and a deep, altirostral skull.
facts.quote: The genus is distinguishable by the combination of these ziphodont teeth and a deep, altirostral skull

facts.statement: Quinkana is typically estimated to be around 3 meters long and weigh around 200 kilograms.
facts.quote: Quinkana is typically estimated to be around 3 m in length and to weigh around 200 kg

facts.statement: Quinkana fossils are predominantly found in sediments preserving woodlands near bodies of water like ponds, streams, and billabongs.
facts.quote: Regardless of its lifestyle and behavior, Quinkana is predominantly found in sediments preserving various types of woodland in proximity to bodies of water such as ponds, streams and billabongs

facts.statement: Paleontologists debate whether Quinkana was terrestrial or semi-aquatic.
facts.quote: The genus has been argued amongst paleontologists to be either terrestrial or semi-aquatic, with both sides providing a variety of arguments

facts.statement: The ecological role of Quinkana in Late Pleistocene Australia is a matter of debate.
facts.quote: The role Quinkana filled in the ecosystems of Late Pleistocene Australia has also been a matter of debate

facts.statement: Some of the earliest fossil finds attributed to Quinkana date back to 1886, when Charles Walter De Vis found bones in the Darling Downs region of Queensland.
facts.quote: Some of the earliest fossil finds now attributed to this genus date as far back as 1886, when Charles Walter De Vis found a variety of fossil bones, including those of Quinkana, in the Darling Downs region of Queensland

facts.statement: Research on Quinkana began in earnest in 1970 when Lyndsey Hawkins discovered fossil material in the Tea Tree Cave in Northern Queensland.
facts.quote: The research history of Quinkana began in earnest in 1970 with the discovery of fossil material in the Tea Tree Cave (part of the Chillagoe caves of Northern Queensland) by Lyndsey Hawkins

facts.statement: A second ziphodont crocodilian was recovered from the Texas Caves in southern Queensland in 1975 by Michael Archer.
facts.quote: Additional discoveries were made in the years following this event, with a second ziphodont crocodilian being recovered from the Texas Caves in southern Queensland in 1975 by Michael Archer

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that Quinkana went extinct due to intense aridification that dried up river basins and destroyed forests, alongside much of Australia's megafauna.
facts.quote: it is hypothesized that another period of intense aridification gradually dried up the river basins and destroyed the forests that the crocodilian inhabited, leading it to go extinct alongside much of Australia's megafauna

facts.statement: Molnar tentatively placed the Texas Cave crocodile within the genus Quinkana but avoided assigning it to a specific species due to potential ontogenetic differences.
facts.quote: Molnar also assigned the Texas Cave crocodile to the genus but was hesitant to make an identification on a species level given some slight differences that may or may not be the result of ontogeny.

facts.statement: Dirk Megirian named the second species, Quinkana timara, in 1994.
facts.quote: in 1994, Quinkana timara was named by paleontologist Dirk Megirian as a second species within the genus

facts.statement: The holotype of Quinkana timara consists of snout fragments found in limestone at the Bullock Creek Locality in the Northern Territory.
facts.quote: The holotype of Q. timara (NTM P895-19) consists of various snout fragments discovered within limestone found in the Bullock Creek Locality in the Northern Territory.

facts.statement: Brian Mackness and Paul M.A. Willis described the third species, Quinkana babarra, two years after Q. timara.
facts.quote: Only two years later a third species of Quinkana, Quinkana babarra, was described, this time by Brian Mackness and Paul M.A. Willis.

facts.statement: Mackness uncovered the maxilla holotype of Quinkana babarra in 1991 at the Dick's Mother Lode Quarry in northeast Queensland.
facts.quote: The holotype (QM F23220), a fragment of the maxilla, was uncovered in 1991 by Mackness at the Dick's Mother Lode Quarry in the Charters Towers Region of northeast Queensland

facts.statement: Quinkana meboldi was discovered in the same year as Q. babarra and formally described in 1997 based on fossils from the White Hunter Site in the Riversleigh World Heritage Area.
facts.quote: The final species to be named was Quinkana meboldi, discovered the same year as Quinkana babarra by Willis. It was described only a year later in 1997 on the basis of multiple maxillary fragments and a partial dentary alongside multiple other mekosuchines from the White Hunter Site of the Riversleigh World Heritage Area

facts.statement: A notable later discovery was a ziphodont tooth of Quinkana found in the Late Pleistocene King Creek catchment on the eastern Darling Downs.
facts.quote: Among the more notable later finds was the discovery of a ziphodont tooth in the Late Pleistocene King Creek catchment of the eastern Darling Downs

facts.statement: Ralph Molnar suggested that Quinkana might have been a terrestrial predator based on its unique cranial anatomy, though he acknowledged counterarguments to this idea.
facts.quote: Based on its unique cranial anatomy, Molnar cautiously proposed that Quinkana could have been a terrestrial predator, though he himself acknowledged several counterarguments to this hypothesis.

facts.statement: Quinkana is best known for its ziphodont teeth, which are inferred for the type species because the holotype fossil lacked preserved teeth in their sockets.
facts.quote: While the genus as a whole is best known for its ziphodont teeth, they are only inferred for the holotype, as the actual fossil did not preserve with any teeth still in their sockets.

facts.statement: The species name fortirostrum combines the Latin words for 'strong' and 'beak' to describe the animal's snout.
facts.quote: The species name was based on the Latin words "fortis" and "rostrum" meaning "strong" and "beak" (in reference to the species' snout) respectively.

facts.statement: Quinkana timara is distinguished from Q. fortirostrum by having a narrower snout and a proportionally larger antorbital shelf.
facts.quote: The species was defined as having a "narrower snout" and "proportionally larger antorbital shelf [opening in the skull]" than Q. fortirostrum.

facts.statement: In 1993, various Australasian fossil crocodilian species, including Quinkana, were placed in the subfamily Mekosuchinae.
facts.quote: various species being described and finally being placed in the subfamily Mekosuchinae in 1993.

facts.statement: Quinkana timara lived during the middle to late Miocene in the Northern Territory of Australia.
facts.quote: Q. timara is known from the Bullock Creek Locality near Camfield Station in Australia's Northern Territory, dating to the middle to late Miocene.

facts.statement: The type species Quinkana fortirostrum lived during the middle Pleistocene in Queensland.
facts.quote: The type species of the genus, Q. fortirostrum was described in 1981 by Ralph Molnar based on a partial skull collected from middle Pleistocene cave deposits in Queensland.

facts.statement: Scientists have repeatedly debated whether Quinkana was terrestrial and its specific role in Australia's prehistoric ecosystems.
facts.quote: During this period the ecology and habits of Quinkana gained more attention, with repeated debate on its role in Australia's prehistoric ecosystems and whether or not it was terrestrial.

facts.statement: The genus name Quinkana is derived from the Quinkans, spirits of the Gugu-Yalanji people of Northern Queensland.
facts.quote: Its generic name was derived from the Quinkans, a type of spirit of the Northern Queensland aboriginal Gugu-Yalanji people.

facts.statement: It is debated whether rock art depicting Quinkans actually shows mekosuchines, as such art is usually interpreted as showing modern crocodile species.
facts.quote: However, it has been noted that though the Quinkans serve as inspiration for the name, no rock art from Australia is actually inferred to depict any mekosuchines, but usually inferred to show the two modern Australian crocodile species.

facts.statement: Quinkana babarra was named in 1996 and is known from the early Pliocene Allingham Formation of Queensland.
facts.quote: Quinkana babarra Named in 1996, this species is known from the early Pliocene Allingham Formation of Queensland but only preserved through a fragment of the maxilla and a few isolated teeth.

facts.statement: Quinkana babarra likely had a wider and shorter snout compared to Q. fortirostrum and Q. timara.
facts.quote: Q. babarra can be differentiated from Q. fortirostrum and Q. timara by likely having a wider and shorter snout.

facts.statement: Quinkana meboldi is the oldest described species of Quinkana, found at the White Hunter Site in Riversleigh, northwestern Queensland, dating to the late Oligocene (ca. 25 Ma).
facts.quote: Quinkana meboldi This species was found at the White Hunter Site in Riversleigh, northwestern Queensland which is a late Oligocene deposit (ca. 25 Ma), making it the oldest species of Quinkana described.

facts.statement: Quinkana meboldi was the only species in the genus that was not ziphodont, possessing partially interlocking teeth without serrations.
facts.quote: In addition to being much more slender-snouted than Quinkana fortirostrum, Quinkana meboldi had partially interlocking teeth that lacked serrations, meaning it was the only species within the genus to not be ziphodont.

facts.statement: Quinkana meboldi was named after Ulrich Mebold, a German astronomer at the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy.
facts.quote: The species was named after Ulrich Mebold, a German astronomer of the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy.

facts.statement: The proportions of Quinkana's snout and its specialized dentition suggest a more terrestrial lifestyle compared to other mekosuchines.
facts.quote: Quinkana is best distinguished from other mekosuchines by the proportions of its snout and its highly specialised dentition, both of which are oftentimes cited as evidence for a more terrestrial lifestyle.

facts.statement: The snout of Q. fortirostrum is deep and angular, resembling proportions found in Paleogene planocraniids and Cretaceous to Miocene sebecosuchians.
facts.quote: The snout of Q. fortirostrum is noticeably deep and angular, its proportions somewhat resembling much older fossil crocodylomorphs such as the planocraniids that existed during the Paleogene across the Northern Hemisphere and the sebecosuchians that were primarily found in South America from the Cretaceous to the Miocene.

facts.statement: The skull of Q. fortirostrum is broader than related fossil groups and distinctly deeper than any modern crocodilian, featuring a trapezoid cross-section.
facts.quote: Molnar describes the skull of Q. fortirostrum as being broader than that of members of the aforementioned groups, yet also distinctly deeper (higher) than those of any modern crocodilians with a distinct trapezoid cross-section.

facts.statement: Q. timara, an older Miocene form, had slender jaws with proportions resembling those of Boverisuchus.
facts.quote: Q. timara, an older form from the Miocene, had noticeably more slender jaws that most closely resemble those of Boverisuchus in proportions.

facts.statement: Q. meboldi had narrower jaws, while Q. babarra had a shorter and broader snout than the Pleistocene Q. fortirostrum.
facts.quote: Q. meboldi had similarly narrower jaws while yet another species, Q. babarra, has been described as having had a shorter and broader snout than even the Pleistocene Q. fortirostrum.

facts.statement: A metatarsal bone found in 1992 at Bluff Downs could belong to Quinkana, but it is equally possible it belonged to a different crocodilian.
facts.quote: A metatarsal bone (QM F30566) was found in 1992 in the Bluff Downs fossil site near Allingham in northern Queensland. This specimen could represent a rare limb element, but it is just as possible that it belonged to a different type of crocodilian altogether.

facts.statement: Researchers Mackness and Sutton tentatively argue that a specific metatarsal does not belong to Q. babarra due to its inferred terrestrial habits, though this remains debated.
facts.quote: Mackness and Sutton, who described the material, tentatively argue that it did not belong to Quinkana babarra on account of the taxon's inferred terrestrial habits, though this is still under debate.

facts.statement: Ristevski and colleagues argue that many isolated teeth traditionally assigned to Quinkana might actually belong to other distinct ziphodont crocodilian genera.
facts.quote: Given the large quantity of ziphodont crocodilians likely to be distinct from Quinkana, Ristevski and colleagues have argued that many isolated teeth traditionally referred to the Quinkana could also belong to these other forms.

facts.statement: Quinkana possessed a deep, vertically oriented skull structure known as altirostral.
facts.quote: The maxillae are steep, which gives the skull of Quinkana its altirostral (deep) appearance.

facts.statement: Quinkana had eyes facing sideways, suggesting it was adapted for a more terrestrial lifestyle than other crocodilians.
facts.quote: The shape of the lacrimal further indicates that Quinkana had eyes that faced sideways rather than up, a hallmark of more terrestrial crocodylomorphs.

facts.statement: Some Quinkana species featured a distinct crest across the upper jaw, with Q. fortirostrum having a rounded crest extending along both the maxilla and premaxilla.
facts.quote: The skull of Q. fortirostrum has a rounded crest which extends along both bones, whereas in Q. timara the crest was restricted entirely to the former.

facts.statement: Quinkana fortirostrum uniquely possessed well-developed knobs on the lacrimal and prefrontal bones, distinct from ridges found in other crocodilians.
facts.quote: Both the lacrimal and prefrontal of Quinkana fortirostrum have well-developed knobs where other crocodilians sometimes have ridges.

facts.statement: Unlike many other crocodilians, the lower jaw of Quinkana lacked the typical wave-like ridges known as festooning.
facts.quote: The bottom of the maxilla is slightly convex and does not display the same pattern of wave-like rises and drops (known as festooning) that is seen in many other crocodilians.

facts.statement: The upper jaw of Quinkana featured only a single notch separating the maxilla and premaxilla bones.
facts.quote: The only notch present in Quinkana is the one separating the maxillae and premaxillae.

facts.statement: Quinkana had a significantly deeper infraorbital bar compared to typical crocodilians, likely providing stronger attachment for jaw muscles.
facts.quote: The depth the maxilla still displays in this region indicates that the infraorbital bar, the region between the lower margin of the eye sockets and the bottom of the cranium, was much deeper than is typical.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the prominent skull knobs in Quinkana fortirostrum were age-related features that developed as the animal grew.
facts.quote: Megirian hypothesizes that age could be a factor in this, with the features changing as the individual grows older.

facts.statement: The palatine bones in Quinkana fortirostrum end between the palatal fenestrae and contact the maxilla via a V-shaped suture.
facts.quote: the palatines in Q. fortirostrum seem to end between the fenestrae where they contact the maxilla via a V-shaped suture.

facts.statement: In Quinkana timara, the fused section of the lower jaw extended back to the sixth dentary tooth.
facts.quote: the mandibular symphysis, the fused section at the tip of the lower jaw, extended back until the sixth dentary tooth.

facts.statement: The teeth of Quinkana are considered truly ziphodont, characterized by lateral compression and serrations.
facts.quote: only those of Quinkana are considered to be truly ziphodont.

facts.statement: In Quinkana fortirostrum, the teeth are inclined to the sides of the maxilla, an orientation best seen ventrolaterally.
facts.quote: In Quinkana fortirostrum for example this orientation is best observed ventrolaterally, meaning the inclination is most obvious when looking at the bottom of the skull from a slight angle.

facts.statement: In Quinkana, front teeth are tall and short horizontally, while rear teeth are lower and longer horizontally.
facts.quote: the teeth towards the front of the jaw tend to be much taller, but are short anteroposteriorly (from the front to the back), whereas the teeth further back are lower but longer horizontally.

facts.statement: Unlike other species, the teeth in Quinkana babarra align in a straight axis.
facts.quote: the axis of the teeth in Q. babarra fall in line with each other.

facts.statement: Quinkana babarra appears to have possessed both serrated and unserrated teeth simultaneously.
facts.quote: Q. babarra meanwhile seems to have had both serrated and unserrated teeth at the same time

facts.statement: The oldest species, Quinkana meboldi, completely lacked serrations on its tooth carinae.
facts.quote: Q. meboldi, the oldest species, lacked serrations on its carinae altogether.

facts.statement: Quinkana meboldi teeth partially interlock like modern crocodiles rather than forming an overbite.
facts.quote: Q. meboldi further stands out from other species in the fact that its teeth do not form an overbite and instead partially interlock more akin to those of modern crocodiles.

facts.statement: Quinkana fortirostrum and Q. timara each had four to five premaxillary teeth and twelve maxillary teeth.
facts.quote: Both Q. fortirostrum and Q. timara are known to have had four to five premaxillary teeth and a further 12 in either maxilla.

facts.statement: Quinkana meboldi had a minimum of 14 maxillary teeth, distinguishing it from younger species.
facts.quote: Q. meboldi is known to have had a minimum of 14 maxillary teeth, setting it apart from the younger species.

facts.statement: Known dentary teeth of Quinkana show elongated and compressed alveoli similar to the upper jaw pattern.
facts.quote: The dentary teeth are poorly understood given the general lack of lower jaw material, but what little is known shows the same overall pattern as those of the upper jaw, with elongated and compressed alveoli.

facts.statement: A single lower jaw fragment suggests one individual of Quinkana could have reached 6 to 7 meters in length.
facts.quote: There is one single bone fragment that could suggest a greater size, with Salisbury and Molnar mentioning a fragment of a lower jaw that could suggest an individual between 6-7 m meters long.

facts.statement: Determining the precise size of Quinkana species is difficult due to a lack of postcranial remains and fragmentary fossils.
facts.quote: The precise size reached by species of the genus Quinkana is a matter of debate, but generally hard to determine both due to the absence of significant postcranial remains and the fragmentary nature of most known material.

facts.statement: Quinkana fortirostrum was originally classified under Crocodylidae in 1981 based on comparisons with other genera.
facts.quote: The type species Q. fortirostrum was originally classified under Crocodylidae in 1981 through comparison against other Eusuchian genera Pristichampsus, Paleosuchus, and Osteolaemus and against the sebecosuchian genus Sebecus.

facts.statement: The subfamily Mekosuchinae was proposed in 1993 by Molnar, Willis, and John Scanlon to group Australian crocodilian genera.
facts.quote: The subfamily Mekosuchinae was proposed in 1993 by Molnar, Willis, and Professor John Scanlon to define this growing number of Australian crocodilian genera.

facts.statement: Willis confirmed the assignment of Quinkana to Mekosuchinae in 1995, noting it was the only family member with ziphodont teeth.
facts.quote: Willis doubled down on the assignment of Quinkana to the Mekosuchinae with a 1995 publication, once again confirming the validity of this grouping despite the fact that Quinkana was the only taxon in the family with ziphodont teeth.

facts.statement: Researchers debate whether size estimates for Quinkana fortirostrum represent maximum lengths or averages, with some arguing the weight was overestimated.
facts.quote: Wroe notes that neither researcher specifies if said estimates are the maximum length or averages while also arguing that the weight appears to have been an overestimate based on the mass of saltwater crocodiles of equal length.

facts.statement: Quinkana is generally classified as a member of the Mekosuchinae subfamily.
facts.quote: the interpretation of Quinkana as a mekosuchine has prevailed as the dominant interpretation

facts.statement: The exact phylogenetic placement of Quinkana within the Mekosuchinae subfamily remains unresolved and has varied across different studies.
facts.quote: the precise position of Quinkana within Mekosuchinae is still not fully resolved and has undergone various incarnations

facts.statement: The discovery of the Q. fortirostrum holotype in cave deposits has been interpreted as evidence that the animal traveled over land before dying.
facts.quote: the discovery of the holotype of Q. fortirostrum in cave deposits is assumed by him to be a strong indicator that the animal traveled over land before falling to its death

facts.statement: Fossil localities containing Quinkana remains often contain a mix of terrestrial and semi-aquatic fauna.
facts.quote: Many of the localities that yielded Quinkana remains show a mix of terrestrial and semi-aquatic fauna

facts.statement: Q. timara is considered the species closest to planocraniids in skull proportions, while Q. fortirostrum is noted for having a much wider head.
facts.quote: Among Quinkana species, Q. timara is perhaps the closest to planocraniids regarding its skull proportions, with Q. fortirostrum standing out as having a much wider head

facts.statement: It is debated whether Quinkana's teeth were used for preying on other crocodilians or for taking down terrestrial prey.
facts.quote: it is just as possible that the teeth may have been used for preying on other crocodilians as it is possible that they were built to take down terrestrial prey

facts.statement: Busbey argued that Quinkana's ziphodont teeth evolved convergently with those of large terrestrial predatory lizards like the Komodo dragon.
facts.quote: Busbey later argued that the ziphodont teeth of Quinkana were developed convergently to those of large, terrestrial predatory lizards such as the komodo dragon

facts.statement: Murray and Vickers-Rich propose that Quinkana was an ambush predator that waited for prey near game trails rather than at the shoreline.
facts.quote: Murray and Vickers-Rich propose that it could have still been an ambush predator, but doing so by waiting for prey near game trails rather than the shoreline

facts.statement: No fossils of the body or limbs have been reliably assigned to Quinkana.
facts.quote: the issue with Quinkana is the lack of fossils representing the body or limbs.

facts.statement: Studies of the related species Kambara suggest it could swing its legs with greater force, offering increased stability, speed, and stride length.
facts.quote: Examinations of the limb bones of Kambara suggest that it was able to swing its legs with much greater force and that the anatomy of various elements gave it increased stability, greater speed and an increased stride length.

facts.statement: It is debated whether hip fossils attributed to Quinkana actually belong to the species, as a clear link between the pelvic material and diagnostic skulls is still missing.
facts.quote: However, until more material showing a clear relation between this pelvic form and Quinkana skull material is found, it cannot be ruled out that the hip fossils belonged to a different mekosuchine.

facts.statement: A popular hypothesis suggests that Australia's top predators in the Pleistocene were primarily reptiles like mekosuchines and giant varanids rather than marsupials.
facts.quote: This had become a popular hypothesis during the later part of the 20th century, proposing that Australia's top predators primarily consisted of reptiles such as mekosuchines, giant varanids and madtsoiid snakes rather than marsupial predators

facts.statement: Stephen Wroe questioned the idea of a reptile-dominated Australia in 2002, arguing that the rarity of reptile remains compared to marsupial remains suggests otherwise.
facts.quote: However, the idea of a reptile-dominated Australia has been questioned by Stephen Wroe in a 2002 publication, casting doubt over the idea and arguing for the contrary, partially due to the apparent rarity of reptile remains compared to those of marsupials.

facts.statement: Some researchers propose that while hunting on land, Quinkana may have retreated to water for protection, thermoregulation, or reproduction.
facts.quote: Some researchers, including Willis and Wroe, have gone on to propose that though hunting on land, Quinkana may have retreated into the water for protection or thermoregulation or even reproduction.

facts.statement: The majority of researchers favor a terrestrial lifestyle for Quinkana, despite acknowledging the limitations of inferring this from skull material alone.
facts.quote: Ultimately, a terrestrial lifestyle has been favored by the majority of researchers, even if they generally acknowledge and highlight the limited information that can be extrapolated from skull material alone.

facts.statement: Quinkana possessed ziphodont teeth that created flattened puncture marks on prey, which are found less frequently than marks made by the crocodilian Baru.
facts.quote: the more flattened punctures that would have been left by Quinkanas ziphodont teeth are noted to be much rarer than those of Baru.

facts.statement: Quinkana lived in environments described as dry vine forests surrounded by scrubs and open woodlands near floodplains.
facts.quote: The Bullock Creek Locality is thought to have once been covered by riparian woodlands as noted by Murray and Vickers-Rich, who describe the paleoenvironment as possibly having been a dry vine forest surrounded by scrubs and more open woodlands that covered the area surrounding the floodplains.

facts.statement: An undetermined species of Quinkana coexisted with Kalthifrons in the Mampuwordu Sands of the Lake Eyre Basin during the Pliocene.
facts.quote: During the Pliocene an undetermined species of Quinkana coexisted with Kalthifrons in the Lake Eyre Basin, specifically the Mampuwordu Sands.

facts.statement: Quinkana babarra lived alongside an undetermined Crocodylus species, a possible Paludirex, and non-crocodilian predators including Thylacoleo, giant snakes, and large monitor lizards.
facts.quote: Q. babarra appeared in the Bluff Downs Local Fauna alongside an undetermined species of Crocodylus and a mekosuchine possibly referrable to Paludirex, while non-crocodilian predators include the marsupial Thylacoleo, giant snakes and large monitor lizards.

facts.statement: During the late Pliocene to middle Pleistocene, Quinkana coexisted with the gharial Gunggamarandu, two species of Paludirex, and an indeterminate Crocodylus species.
facts.quote: Even more recent rock layers of the late Pliocene to middle Pleistocene saw Quinkana coexist with the gharial Gunggamarandu, both Paludirex vincenti and Paludirex gracilis, a possible third Paludirex species and an indeterminate species of Crocodylus.

facts.statement: At King Creek, Quinkana coexisted with Megalania and megafauna such as Protemnodon, Macropus titan, Diprotodon, and Troposodon, though it was likely rare in eastern Queensland.
facts.quote: At King Creek Quinkana is known to have coexisted with Megalania and a wide range of potential prey items including Protemnodon, Macropus titan and other kangaroos, Diprotodon and Troposodon, though it is noted that it was likely rare in eastern Queensland relative to other parts of Australia.

facts.statement: Fossils of Quinkana found at South Walker Creek in Western Queensland were recovered alongside 16 other megafauna species, only three of which survive today.
facts.quote: Another Late Pleistocene river deposit, South Walker Creek in Western Queensland, recovered Quinkana material alongside 16 other species of megafauna, only three of which are still extant.

facts.statement: The range of Quinkana was closely linked to freshwater systems surrounded by riparian woodlands and vine forests where it shared the habitat with many other crocodilians.
facts.quote: Overall, the range of Quinkana, whether it was terrestrial or not, appears to have been closely linked to freshwater systems, in particular those surrounded by riparian woodland and vine forests, typically sharing this environment with a plethora of other crocodilians.

facts.statement: Quinkana survived a major wave of extinction that wiped out other mekosuchines like Baru, suggesting its ecology differed significantly from those that perished.
facts.quote: this burst of aridification does not appear to have affected Quinkana greatly. Remains of this genus are found before and after the proposed late Miocene extinctions, which has been taken as potential evidence for its ecology differing significantly from the taxa that went extinct.

facts.statement: Quinkana survived until the Late Pleistocene, with fossils dating from 122,000 years ago at King Creek and 40,000 to 20,000 years ago at South Walker Creek.
facts.quote: Fossil evidence suggests that Quinkana survived until the Late Pleistocene, with records from that time including the isolated tooth of King Creek, dated to be around 122,000 years old, and the fossils recovered from the South Walker Creek site that have been dated to be from around 40,000 to 20,000 years ago.

facts.statement: Research suggests hydroclimactic conditions in eastern Australia deteriorated abruptly around 48,000 years ago, leading to the extinction of Quinkana.
facts.quote: According to them, the hydroclimactic conditions began to deteriorate abruptly around 48,000 years ago in the Lake Eyre Basin, with the other river basins of eastern Australia following suit within the next eight thousand years.

facts.statement: Researchers argue that human arrival was likely coincidental to Quinkana's extinction because the timing of megafauna extinction contradicts the pattern expected if humans were the primary driver.
facts.quote: The arrival of humans, though falling into the same time frame, was likely coincidental and not tied to the extinction of Quinkana, as the team argues that the extinction of Australia's megafauna runs in the opposite direction of what would be expected should humans have been the primary driver.

facts.statement: While rapid human hunting is disputed, some researchers suggest a more gradual human-influenced extinction could have occurred through habitat destruction via cultural burning.
facts.quote: The team does however point out that this does not necessarily preclude a more gradual human-influenced extinction, which may have involved habitat destruction via cultural burning.

facts.statement: The extinction of Quinkana marked the disappearance of the last archosaur lineage possessing ziphodont dentition.
facts.quote: The extinction of Quinkana meant the disappearance of the last archosaur lineage with ziphodont dentition.

facts.statement: The genus Quinkana was named by Molnar in 1981.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Molnar, 1981

facts.statement: Quinkana was an extinct Mekosuchine crocodile that lived in Australia from about 24 million years ago until about 40,000 years ago.
facts.quote: Quinkana es un género extinto de cocodrilo mekosuquino que vivió en Australia desde hace unos 24 millones de años hasta hace unos 40.000 años

facts.statement: During the Pleistocene, Quinkana was one of Australia's large terrestrial predators, characterized by elongated limbs and ziphodont teeth that were laterally compressed, recurved, and serrated.
facts.quote: En el Pleistoceno Quinkana fue uno de los grandes depredadores terrestres de Australia, dotado de extremidades alargadas y dientes zifodontes (comprimidos lateralmente, recurvados y aserrados)

facts.statement: The name Quinkana is derived from the "Quinkans," a legendary people from Australian Aboriginal mythology.
facts.quote: El nombre Quinkana viene de los "Quinkans", un pueblo legendario de los mitos de los aborígenes australianos

facts.statement: The type species Q. fortirostrum lived in Queensland during the Pliocene and Pleistocene epochs.
facts.quote: Q. fortirostrum de Queensland del Plioceno y el Pleistoceno

facts.statement: The species Q. babarra lived in Queensland during the early Pliocene.

facts.statement: The species Q. timara lived in the Northern Territory during the mid-Miocene.
